Title: A Solution to the Lost Position - Out of Game Considerations Problem.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Since the activity of a player in a lost position can have more effect
on the game than it "should" (from some perspectives), especially,
apparently, cross-table attacks (from some "out of game"
considerations"), I offer this solution:

Extend "ousted' to include "in a lost position". That is, if a
Methuselah has succeeded in getting xer prey into a lost position,
then xe is credited with the oust and that lost position Methuselah
immediately and spontaneously is ousted.

The actual mechanics go like this: if a Methuselah initiates any
activity (or "pass") that seems (to any player at the table) to
indicate that Methuselah is not Playing to Win (that is, xe is working
toward zero more VPs), ask for explanation. If xe indicates that xe is
not in violation of the Play to Win rules because xe is in a lost
position, then call a judge over to confirm. If the judge agrees, then
xe is ousted (predator gets 1VP and six pool as usual).

(If not, of course, then the PTW-violating activity (or pass) is
voided and prohibited, and the Methuselah must make some PTW activity,
as usual.)

<begin smilie block>
This has the added benefit that a Methuselah won't have xer VP
"stolen" by getting ousted after xe has put xer prey in a lost
position but before xe can actually reduce xer prey's pool to zero.
<end smilie block>

This would be better than the current rules (at least, the crosstable
players would be safe), but this wouldn't solve the rest problems. The
level of interaction between players (their ability to prevent gaining
VP) is going to fall to zero, as even Life Boon wouldn't help. The
game shifts could potentially be even more sudden and surprising,
since transferring out can burn only 4 pool per turn, while immedtiate
ousting would burn it all. I don't think that's good.
If you're looking for the simple solution, what prevents you from
simply prohibiting the "lost position" rulings? I don't think that
many players would be harmed for having to wait a few minutes until
somebody ousts them.

> <begin smilie block>
> This has the added benefit that a Methuselah won't have xer VP
> "stolen" by getting ousted after xe has put xer prey in a lost
> position but before xe can actually reduce xer prey's pool to zero.
> <end smilie block>

As long as this joke seems to be related to my example, I should
confirm that I can see the difference between "completely disabling
your prey" and "completely disabling the whole table" :) Thus, if a
player disabled his prey but not his predator, the predator can (and
even should) oust both him and his prey. This isn't "stealing", it's
normal game.
BTW, I still remember the times of Dramatic Upheaval and Kindred
Restructure. Then there were a lot of players who also didn't believe
that switching places was actually stealing other players' VPs :)

There always are people who prefer the status quo - as there were
people who liked PTO and Upheavals.
But I've got another simple solution: the virtual Life Boon! :)
As long as the judge confirms that the player is in the "lost
position", the judge decides how much pool would the player need to
continue playing. Then, the judge starts the auction, in which players
are bidding pool for the "Life Boon". The winning player gives that
much pool to the poor, and follows all the rules of Life Boon. Only if
nobody is willing to pay that much the player is really ousted.
What's not to like here?

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
Why not just change the Play to Win rules to say that if you can't get
any more VP's, you have to play to maximize your tournament points?
That is, if you can't get more VP's, try to get the highest possible
ranking at the table.

It's pretty simple, and it gives players who can get no more VP's a
justifiable reason to poolsack/self-oust/cross-table rush, etc.
WITHOUT taking into account out-of-game factors.

I think this rules change would go a long way in resolving the
ambiguity surrounding the issue of the best way to act in a "hopeless"
situation.

It would affect table interaction positively, since a "hopeless"
player can honestly appeal to the table: if you all don't help me, my
position becomes impossible, and I will assist the winning player to
try to tie for second/third/last place. No spite involved, just
calculation.

Messages.Author: XZealot
Messages.Body:
> Honestly, I still do not get the idea behind the current rule.  What I
> gather is that the rule enforces the value that players should have
> the freedom to choose how they lose as well as how they win.  As I
> said I don't share this value as implemented, if that is indeed the

The rule reinforces that players play by the rules and the spirit of
the game, namely oust your prey and gain a VP until you have the
majority of VPs.

As opposed to how previous to this ruling, when I player could justify
that he could no longer gain a VP prior to his death (no matter how
far that death is away), he was exempted from his social contract with
the other players at the game to "have fun" through "mutual
competition to attain a previously agreed upon goal, to get the GW,
which in turn allowed him to "have fun" by substituting a new goal of
his own choosing. Often this created arbitrary and capricious plays.

Now when it is determined that a player no longer is pursuing the
mutually agreed upon goal of trying to win the game then that player
is removed from competition.

Messages.Author: smithson
Messages.Body:
I know there's a bunch of threads currently up on this subject, but I
am still having trouble understanding the vague guidelines behind the
PTW rules. Where is the threshold for "reasonable"? What is a "lost"
position? What are the requirements for going for VPs? It seems
anything that would reduce your pool to 0 would be illegal under PTW,
since there's always a chance (albeit slim) for at least the 0.5 VP
from withdrawing. Likewise, if the threshold for "reasonable" is
higher, if I sat at a table and knew the other decks and decided that
I didn't have a chance to win, wouldn't I be able to immediately
declare myself "lost" and then act in whatever fashion I wanted? Or if
someone plays a Kpist m/45 can I say he's not playing to win, since .
44 is better (and he shouldn't have had a worse card in his deck)?
What if someone votes for/against a referendum? Can I have a judge
question his decision based on how I think he should best be following
the PTW rule?

I know that's an extreme (and silly) example, but it seems to me like
the judge in events not only has to correctly make card rulings, but
can be forced into making rulings about play in the game. I recently
read a tournament report where in the final table, all players agreed
to gang up on one person (who was running an Una deck). Now, if all
players working in concert to take out one can be considered valid
under PTW, what's stopping one person working cross-table? If I'm
playing a rush deck, I could just simply say that in my estimation,
Player X (who's crosstable) is a threat to me, and I need to weaken
him. Does the judge get to overrule me? And if he can, why would going
crosstable be allowed in the tourney report I read? Do the players at
the table get to decide?

I know a lot of this probably rarely comes up in actual tournaments,
but if it's even an issue 10% of the time, that seems like it can
really be causing games to not reward "good" play.

Assuming you're serious: there is a huge grey area on the border of
legality already. I've very seldom seen judges effectively dealing
with instances of slow play, of stalling, of deck stacking, of
collusion, etc. (things that happen probably every single tournament).

you are not in a lost position, how you can still win, what card
you hope to draw... Not convinced.

So this is the smilie block. So the rest was serious, I guess.

Messages.Author: Wilsoros
Messages.Body:
I firmly believe that if you feel that PTW does not need to be
updated, then you do not play in tournaments of any consequence.

Got your attention? good

Like porn we all know bullshit when we see it, we see the "I can't win
so I can lose how I want" that is what we are talking about here. I
can't win, so I am ousted, period, no longer any "oh LSJ says I can
lose how I want" as soon as you feel you can't play to win, then you
should be ousted. We're talking sportsmanship here, it isn't an
unambiguous definition, and rarely is it black and white, but our goal
is a fair and fun environment, so given the multiplayer nature, we
need to ensure it.

If you feel you can't win, you can still "lie" and say you have a shot
and rush cross table, do all the stupid things you think of, the only
difference is you may be asked to explain privately to a judge why you
are doing what you are doing.

What this rule is offering is a sportsmanship route of self-ousting
when you know the game is lost and you want everyone else to keep
fighting it out.

Exactly. The new rule would at least force people to play by the
spirit of the rules. All too often I've seen people do crazy,
capricious things crosstable (often out of spite), just because they
currently can do that "when in a losing position". Also, in my opinion
many people tend to have a *very* weird view of what a "losing
position" is, and decide that they can't win at a very early stage.
This rule would force them to think hard about that position, and if
they really think they are in a losing position then they could not
disrupt the rest of the game by some capricious stunt (to help a
friend, or whatever).

"judge!" calls before people adjust.

stay in the game as long as possible, but since enforcing something
like that is next to impossible I think LSJ's proposal is the next
best thing.

Petri Wessman <or...@orava.org> wrote:
>But the hole, as I see it, is in the fact that a player who is in a
>"lost" position (i.e. cannot get more VPs in any reasonable fashion)

>crosstable action "just to cycle cards" or "just because", often
>claiming their justification in "I can do whatever I want, since I can
>no longer get VPs" (which *is* technically true, currently).

If a player is in a position where they can cause significant problems
for people in this fashion, it's entirely possible that they can strike
a deal on the table.

Assume a standard A, B, C, D, E table. I think I'm in a lost position,
and so decide to rush D because C is my friend (or for any other
reason). If I'm in a position to do that, it's quite likely I can turn
to C and say "Hi C, how about I send D's vampire(s) to torpor, and you
Kindred Spirits bleed B for me? That should make your life easier for
getting VPs, and I might be able to oust B."

That is, if your players are being capable of being significantly
disruptive to the game but think they're close to being in a lost
position / in a lost position then:

- that player should consider negotiating with other players as to which
actions he should take, potentially playing for a time-out or an
unlikely oust

- the other players should consider negotiating with the lost
Methuselah, in order to make sure that they have sensible avenues to
pursue.

If I, methuselah A, see C locking down D with a bunch of Sensory
Deprivations, and I think that's going to edge towards putting D in a
lost position, it's perfectly sensible for me to deal with D and banish
C's Gabrin. I get something out of it - D isn't lost, and doesn't self-
oust and help C, and I get pressure on my predator (E).

If your players are finding themselves with many Methuselahs in lost
positions who want to self-oust or otherwise act in fashions that cause
problems (for that Methuselah), perhaps your players would do well to
consider that they're in a multi-player game. Cross-table assistance,
alliances, dealing, meddling, double-crossing, screwing over,
blackmailing and so on are intentional parts of the game.

If you don't want a player to act arbitrarily and prevent you from
winning, throw that player a bone. Better for you to get 3VPs than
none.

It's not a common occurrence, in fact over here it's quite rare, and
only seen in tournaments. And I think everyone is quite aware that
this is a multiplayer game, thankyouverymuch. :}

The problem is that when it comes up, it's ugly to deal with (as a
judge), especially in the current climate where nobody seems to be
quite sure what's acceptable and what's not. That's why I'd love to
see more clarification on the issue.

Sure, the smart thing for a player with crosstable actions would be to
try to get some deal out of it. But what if he doesn't want to do that
and just wants to dick around, saying "I can do whatever I want, since
I'm in a losing position". At what point can a judge step in and say
"you can't do that"?

Relatedly, what is a "losing position" anyway, officially? If you take
the hardline approach, there pretty much is no such animal, since it's
always possible the game state may change unexpectedly in a way which
would let you get the 0,5VP, at least. Which would mean that it's
never actually legal to transfer out.

Since people generally seem to think it's ok to transfer out in some
cases... what are those cases?

I'm not trying to be anal here, I'm just trying to get a grip on how
to judge the issue, if it comes up in tournaments.

-Petri

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
Petri Wessman <or...@orava.org> wrote:
>If you by that you mean "things you have written in this thread", that
>still doesn't totally enlighten me. By what I gather, the only
>official definition of "lost position" is "one in which the player has
>no reasonable chance of getting a GW or more VPs".
>
>...and the definition of "reasonable" is equally vague (as per the
>dictionary definition).

Consider a situation where two players on a table strike a VP splitting
deal. And for the sake of argument, it includes one of those players
getting 3VP first and then - because they have the game win and don't
have to maximize VPs beyond the GW - they say they'll roll over and give
the other player 2VP. (This basically involves two players who are sat
next to each other, although I think Life Boon could probably come into
play too.)

A third player calls the judge over and says that he thinks the 2VP
player is striking a losing deal, in violation of PTW, because he thinks
that that player is giving up a good chance at a game win for himself.

The judge looks at the table and makes a judgment on whether it's a
legal deal or not.

How does the judge do this? Using his or her understanding of V:TES,
the judge decides if the chances suggested are reasonable and if the
players are making reasonable choices. A player is not obligated to
play for a tiny, tiny, tiny 0.00001% chance of a GW in the qualifying
rounds[0], because it can - quite reasonably - backfire and cause him to
lose the reasonable option of gaining VPs because he turned down a deal,
or something. What's the threshold for when such behaviour becomes
illegal? The judge's opinion on what is reasonable.

If your judges can judge what is reasonable in a deal-making
environment, why is it so hard for them to judge what is reasonable in a
lost position? They're capable of deciding that something is too remote
a possibility to force a player to fight for it in a deal making
scenario. Why can't they do the same when judging a lost position?

Your judges *are* enforcing the play to win rules on deals, yes?

[0] In the final, a player can't make their position worse in the same
way - either they get a GW, or they come joint second. In joint second,
the number of VPs they have from earlier or their previous standing
isn't relevant. So in the final, the players should always try to get a
GW because it can't backfire. (Obviously, they can bide their time for
a better chance at a GW rather than leaping for it frivolously now.)

In this sort of situation, it's quite useful for the tournament
organizer/head judge to spend a minute just before the first round
briefly outlining any troublesome potential issues, and asking players
to come and talk to them if they have any issues, or call them over
during a game etc.

When grouping was new to the game, I remember reminding players about it
at the next few tournaments. At many tournaments, I've asked players to
try to make sure they differentiate between referendum negotiations
before a block and referendum negotiations once the referendum is
called. (Having run into a few too many problems where player A says
they're in the referendum, and player B says they're not so wants to
block.) A short description of play to win is perfectly sensible, if
it's a common cause of concerns.
